title: Making Grocery Delivery Profitable
prompt: Your client is an online grocer that loses money on every delivery. They want to make delivery profitable without hurting the customer experience. How would you approach it?
background: The grocer delivers orders to customers' homes from local stores/warehouses.
Average order value is $80, at a 30% gross margin (so $24 of margin per order).
Delivery currently costs more than that margin.
They don't want to degrade delivery speed/quality for customers.

clarifying_answers.What is the goal: Make the delivery operation at least break even per order.
clarifying_answers.What is the margin per order: AOV $80 x 30% gross margin = $24 of margin per order, before delivery cost.
clarifying_answers.Is volume the problem: No — demand is fine; the unit economics of delivery are the problem.
clarifying_answers.Any constraints: Keep delivery windows reasonable; don't gut service quality.

exhibits.name: Delivery Cost per Order
exhibits.description: What it costs to deliver one order today.
exhibits.data: Delivery cost per order $30: driver labor $18, fuel/vehicle $6, picking/packing $6.

exhibits.name: Route Density
exhibits.description: Driver productivity drives the labor cost.
exhibits.data: A driver is paid $200/day (8 hours) and currently completes ~11 deliveries/day (low route density). If density doubled to ~22 deliveries/day, driver cost per delivery would roughly halve.

good_framework: Profit per order = gross margin − delivery cost; delivery cost splits into labor, fuel/vehicle, picking/packing.
Labor per delivery is driven by route density (deliveries per driver per day) — the biggest lever.
Levers: densify routes (delivery windows, minimum order, zone batching), raise AOV / add a delivery fee, optimize picking.
Quantify the flip to profitability; protect service quality.

quant.question: What is the current profit (or loss) per order?
quant.work: $24 margin − $30 delivery cost = −$6 per order (a loss).

quant.question: If route density doubles (11 → 22 deliveries/day), what is the new labor cost per delivery and the new profit per order?
quant.work: $200/day ÷ 22 ≈ $9 labor per delivery (down from $18, saving ~$9). New delivery cost ~$21; $24 − $21 = +$3 per order.

quant.question: If they also raise AOV to $100 (margin $30), what is profit per order at the denser routes?

recommendation: The loss is driven mainly by low route density inflating driver labor ($18 of the $30 cost). Densifying routes — tighter delivery windows, minimum order sizes, and zone batching — roughly halves labor per delivery and flips the unit economics from −$6 to about +$3 per order on its own. Layering in a higher minimum/AOV (and a modest delivery fee) pushes it to ~+$9. Recommend a densification program first, protecting service with scheduled windows, then AOV levers.
